title: The Feature Search Bar
takeaway: A screenshot of the search strip in the paper's public feature browser, with its four dropdowns opened. It carries no results, so what it establishes is only the shape of the query the authors built for themselves: pick a matching mode, pick which part of a feature's record the query is matched against, pick a sort key over all features in a run, and pick which per-token loss difference is drawn as underlines.
walkthrough:
### What you are looking at

One strip of controls from the [[feature-exploration-interface]], the published viewer that covers every [[feature]] in every [[dictionary-learning-run]]. The four menus are shown opened, stacked below the bar they belong to. The three arrows and their captions at the top, and the two paragraphs at the right, are annotations the paper added to the screenshot.

No feature, no dataset example and no number appears here. Read it as a description of a query, not as evidence.

### How to read it

Left to right, the row builds one search. The first box takes a string, and the menu beside it says how that string is matched: literally, ignoring case, as a regular expression, or as a whole-field match rather than a substring.

The "in" menu says which part of a feature's record the string is matched against. Options span the [[top-dataset-examples]] a feature fires on, the tokens of those examples on their own, the feature's [[logit-weight]] entries, its index and name, and the explanation written for it by [[automated-interpretability]].

"Sort by" then orders the features. Some keys are plain bookkeeping — index, random. Others are properties the paper measures elsewhere: how strongly a feature fires at most, its [[feature-density]], and how close it sits to a single neuron, which is the check behind [[feature-neuron-nonalignment]].

### What it shows

The last menu is the one that carries real content. Under "Feature Ablation", each token's underline is coloured by the change in that token's predicted log-likelihood when this one feature's contribution is subtracted from the MLP activation — replacing $\mathbf{x}$ with $\mathbf{x} - f_i(\mathbf{x})\mathbf{d}_i$ and finishing the forward pass. That is [[feature-ablation]], read per token.

Under "Residual Ablation", nothing is switched off. The whole MLP activation is replaced by the autoencoder's reconstruction from all learned features, and the underline shows the resulting loss difference. It is the per-token view of the global claim that the dictionary recovers most, not all, of what the MLP contributes; see [[loss-recovered-by-features]].

So the strip mostly tells you what the authors wanted to be able to ask: find features by their behaviour, then look at what each one is worth to the loss.

terms.definition: The free-text box at the far left, with a "Go" button. The string typed here is matched against whichever part of a feature's record the "in" menu selects.

The default matching mode: the query string must appear in the searched field with exactly the capitalisation typed. Relevant here because many features in this paper key on case and on script, so "the" and "The" can belong to different features.
Matching mode that ignores capitalisation, so a query matches upper- and lower-case occurrences alike.
Treats the query as a regular expression rather than a literal string, matching with capitalisation respected. Useful for finding character classes, such as runs of digits or non-Latin script.
The same regular-expression matching, with capitalisation ignored.
Requires the searched field to equal the query in full, rather than merely containing it. Distinguishes a token that is exactly the query from any longer token containing it.
The label above the second menu. It selects which part of each feature's stored record the query is matched against.

Search field option: match the query against the text of the dataset examples on which a feature activates most strongly. These top-activating examples are the standard first-pass way of guessing what a unit responds to.

Search field option: match against the individual tokens of those top examples rather than the surrounding text, so a hit means the feature fired on or near that specific token rather than somewhere in the same passage.

Search field option: match against the vocabulary tokens a feature pushes up or down when it fires, rather than against the contexts where it fires. This searches by what a feature does instead of when it activates.
Search field option: match against both the top activating examples and the logit-affected tokens, returning features that hit in either.
Search field option: match against the individual tokens of the top examples together with the logit-affected tokens.
Search field option: match against a feature's numeric index within its run and any name attached to it, which is how you jump straight to a feature you already know, such as A/1/3450.

Search field option: match against the natural-language explanation a language model wrote for the feature from examples of its activations. Searching this field means searching the machine-written descriptions rather than the raw data.
The label above the third menu. It chooses the ordering applied to the features listed, independently of the search itself.

The default sort key, and the interface's own label for some measure of how consistently a feature fires on similar inputs. The paper's text does not define it, so treat the name as the only description available.

Sort keys ordering features by the largest value the feature ever reaches, descending or ascending. A feature's maximum activation is the scale the paper uses elsewhere when it divides a feature's range into intervals.

Sort keys ordering features by feature density, the fraction of tokens on which the feature is nonzero. "Min Dense" surfaces the rarest features, which the paper associates with an ultralow-density cluster that is mostly uninterpretable.

terms.term: Max Neuron Aligned / Min Neuron Aligned
terms.definition: Sort keys ordering features by how close a feature is to being a single MLP neuron. This is the property the paper checks when it argues a feature is not merely a relabelled neuron; the exact statistic behind the menu entry is not stated in the text.
Sort key ordering by the ratio of a feature's maximum activation to its density, which favours features that fire rarely but hard.
Sort key ordering features by their position in the dictionary, which is arbitrary with respect to meaning and serves as a stable default ordering.
Sort key giving an arbitrary shuffle. It matters for evaluation, because judging features only by the most striking ones is the bias the paper's blinded scoring is designed to avoid.
Sort key ordering by how well each feature matches the typed query. It is greyed out in this screenshot because the search box is empty, so no relevance ranking exists yet.
Sort key ordering features by how well a machine-written explanation predicts the feature's true activations, scored as a rank correlation between predicted and actual values.
The label above the fourth menu. It selects which quantity is used to colour the underline drawn beneath each token in the displayed text examples.

Underline mode: colour each token by the change in its predicted log-likelihood when this single feature's contribution is subtracted from the MLP activation and the forward pass is completed. It shows which predictions depended on this one feature.

Underline mode: colour each token by the loss difference when the MLP activation is replaced wholesale by the autoencoder's reconstruction from all learned features. It shows where the dictionary as a whole fails to reproduce the layer.
Underline mode that draws no underlines, leaving only the activation highlighting on the text.
The unit vector in MLP activation space along which a feature writes when it fires, written $\mathbf{d}_i$. Ablation subtracts the activation times this direction.

terms.term: "Search among the features" / "Where the search query is matched" / "Which ablation is used to color the underlines of tokens"
terms.definition: The three arrow captions across the top. They are labels the paper added to the screenshot, not text present in the interface.

numbers.meaning: Matching modes offered for the query string: case sensitive, case insensitive, two regular-expression variants, and exact (not substring).
Fields the query can be matched against: top examples, top example tokens, logits, the two combinations of those, index and name, and autointerpretation.
Sort keys listed, of which one (Search Relevance) is disabled because no query has been entered.
Underline modes: Feature Ablation, Residual Ablation, and None.
The number of features switched off under "Feature Ablation" — exactly one, the feature currently being viewed. This is what separates it from Residual Ablation, where no feature is removed at all.

The fraction of the MLP's log-likelihood loss reduction recovered by the features in run A/1, the run the paper focuses on. "Residual Ablation" is the per-token picture of the remaining 21%: the loss the reconstruction fails to account for.
The complementary share — the extra loss incurred by replacing the MLP activations with the autoencoder's output, measured against the loss from zero-ablating the MLP entirely.

The higher recovery figure for run A/5, which uses 131,072 learned features and an L1 coefficient of 0.004. Given as evidence that the residual shrinks with a larger dictionary or a weaker sparsity penalty, so what a Residual Ablation underline shows depends on which run you are browsing.
The number of tokens in the subset of the training dataset from which the interface's displayed examples are drawn, with only 10 tokens taken from each context.
Tokens of context shown on each side of the selected token in the interface's text windows — the span across which these underlines are drawn.
The count of results, activations, features or measurements visible in this screenshot. The figure documents the query controls only.
